stories.title: Green Street Expands Student Housing Data Platform
stories.excerpt: Investors eyeing student housing assets have a newly expanded study tool. College House, a destination for specialized data and analytics on the U.S. student housing sector, is officially offering investors and operators direct access to analytics firm Green Street’s investment analytics. The platform expansion launched on Tuesday, a little more than a year after Green Street acquired College House in 2025. The news comes amid a complicated cooling period for the U.S. student housing market, according to Green Street’s own 2026 student housing report. Asset values have declined recently due to rising cap rates, while revenue growth is expected to average just 2 percent over the next two years, slightly trailing apartments. Capital is returning to student housing, according to commercial real estate finance firm Walker & Dunlop’s annual outlook, but is similarly selective, and activity remains below 2022 peaks. Construction starts are slowing and deliveries are highly concentrated, with the market splitting along enrollment trends. College House users can now tap Green Street estimates tailored to the student housing market within its platform, including key metrics like cap rates, risk-adjusted return estimates, occupancy and supply. The announcement also introduced a proprietary scoring framework, dubbed University Grades, that identifies long-term rent growth potential for nearly 180 U.S. schools. “This is exactly the integration we envisioned when we acquired College House,” Andrew McCulloch, chief analytics officer of Green Street, said in a statement. “Combining Green Street’s independent research and proprietary valuation framework with College House’s best-in-class data assets, will provide student housing investors a complete toolkit to allocate capital more effectively.” Time for investors to hit the books. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.

stories.title: Developer Eyeing 143-Acre “Italian Village” in Prosper
stories.excerpt: BlackStone Communities is prodding the town of Prosper to adopt its plans to recreate an Italian Village. The Marco, a proposed 143-acre mixed-use development, is slated for the northeast corner of the Dallas North Tollway and US 380. Community Impact reports plans for the development include a public square, retail, single-family and multifamily housing, a performing arts venue and a hotel, all centered around a lagoon with canals big enough to navigate by boat. Marco’s defining feature is its lagoon and canals, which span over 15 acres. The Marco features a mix of housing options with the total number of residential units capped at 4,400. They include: Mid-rise apartments: maximum 2,500 units High-rise residential (condominiums or apartments): maximum 400 units Retirement community: maximum 500 units The Marco also includes a significant office, commercial and entertainment component. In addition to office condos for smaller companies, conceptual plans for The Marco show two larger campuses with separate parking designated for corporate headquarters. stories.title: Lone Star PACE Facilitates Nearly $65M in Loans for 6 Texas Projects
stories.excerpt: Lone Star PACE closed on $64.8 million in Texas PACE Program financing during the first half of 2026, supporting approximately $279 million in commercial real estate investment while helping property owners significantly reduce energy and water consumption. The six closed transactions span a diverse mix of property types, including hospitality, retail, industrial, data centers and specialty development, demonstrating the growing role of Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy (C-PACE) financing in helping developers strengthen project capital stacks while incorporating high-performance building systems. Projects financed during the first half of the year include the Holiday Inn Express in Pilot Point, MCM Elegante in Beaumont (shown), Ashford Yard in Houston, Cold Storage Seabrook, Vesgro Data Center in Irving and Maranello Luxury Garages in Plano. The Texas PACE Program enables property owners and developers to finance qualifying energy and water conservation improvements through a voluntary property assessment. C-PACE financing can fund up to 35% of a project’s capital stack and may be used for new construction, redevelopment and retrofit projects. stories.title: Triten Snags Refi on 342-Unit Houston Rental Community
stories.excerpt: Triten Real Estate Partners obtained refinancing for The Mill Residences, a 342-unit mid-rise multifamily community located at 2315 Navigation Blvd. in the East End of Houston, Texas. Northmarq’s Warren Hitchcock and Taylor Phillips arranged the refinance loan on behalf of Triten. Northmarq’s Hitchcock added. “Northmarq secured a creative and flexible refinance prior to final stabilization which replaced the construction loan, provided additional capital for the retail buildout, and gave Triten the runway needed to complete the property’s business plan.” The Mills Residences offers a mix of class A studio, one-, two-bedroom apartments. Amenities such as a fitness center, yoga studio, poolside cabanas and a quiet lounge equipped with high-speed connectivity designed for remote workers. Built in 2025, the multifamily community places residents at the center of Houston’s East End, providing residents with convenient access to public transit, dining, live entertainment and the area’s growing arts district.  The post Triten Snags Refi on 342-Unit Houston Rental Community appeared first on Connect CRE.

stories.title: Cybersecurity Tracker SecurityScorecard Renews 1140 Avenue of the Americas Lease
stories.excerpt: A cybersecurity risk management firm is renewing its Midtown office space, Commercial Observer has learned. SecurityScorecard signed a five-year renewal on its 8,475-square-foot space at 1140 Avenue of the Americas, owned by American Strategic Investment Company, where it has been since 2023, according to tenant broker JLL. The asking rent was not immediately disclosed, but the average office asking rent in Midtown in the second quarter of 2026 was $86.18 per square foot, according to a CBRE report. “SecurityScorecard is experiencing tremendous momentum as organizations around the world increasingly rely on our platform to manage cyber risk across their digital ecosystems,” Aleksandr Yampolskiy, CEO and founder of SecurityScorecard, said in a statement. “Renewing our headquarters at 1140 Avenue of the Americas reflects our long-term commitment to the city and provides our team with a workplace that supports continued growth, innovation and collaboration.” JLL’s Valentin Stobetsky negotiated on behalf of the tenant, while Josh Kuriloff, Matthias Li, Heather Thomas, Pierce Hance and Nicole Estevez of Cushman & Wakefield handled the deal for the landlord. “It has a premier Midtown location, outstanding transit access, modern amenities and a unique full-floor office with an expansive private outdoor terrace that enhances the employee experience,” Stobetsky said in a statement. Li echoed the sentiment that the Midtown market and the building’s premium offerings would aid the company in its expansion. C&W did not immediately respond to a request for additional comment. The landlord, which also goes by American Realty Capital New York City REIT or New York City REIT, arranged a lease at the same tower for Epic Insurance in February, when the company took 25,500 square feet. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.

stories.title: Hilton-Branded Hotel Offerings to Anchor Former Nashville Office Tower
stories.excerpt: Office space in the downtown Fifth Third Center is slated to be converted into hundreds of hotel and timeshare units. The Nashville Business Journal reports that the rooms will be part of Hilton’s LXR Hotels & Resorts brand and Hilton Grand Vacations. Pivot Real Estate Partners and Hastings Architecture are helming the conversion of the 30-story tower. The tower, located at 424 Church St., is slated to offer a total of 483 rooms, including 318 hotel rooms and 165 timeshare units. Other features of the future hotel and timeshare tower include separate amenity spaces for hotel guests and timeshare owners, as well as a ballroom. A lobby bar, all-day restaurant and retail and coffee space are planned for the building’s ground level. The building’s plaza is planned to feature an outdoor bar with a food-and-beverage concept. Pivot Real Estate Partners bought Fifth Third Center for $55.25 million last August. The post Hilton-Branded Hotel Offerings to Anchor Former Nashville Office Tower appeared first on Connect CRE.

stories.title: Arrow Adds Veteran Multifamily Lender Ari Mandelbaum to Grow Platform
stories.excerpt: Arrow Real Estate Advisors continues to ramp up its roster nearly two years after its founding. The capital markets advisory firm founded by Morris Betesh in fall 2024 has added Ari Mandelbaum, a former lender at Greystone and Dwight Capital, as a director to help grow its multifamily debt placement business, Commercial Observer has learned. “Ari brings a highly valuable perspective to Arrow given his extensive experience on the lender side of the business,” Betesh said in a statement. “His understanding of underwriting, credit and execution allows him to approach financing assignments from both sides of the table and provide clients with a deeper level of insight throughout the capital-raising process.” Mandelbaum previously held senior roles at Greystone and Dwight Capital specializing in agency and bridge loans across multifamily and other property sectors. He was at Greystone from 2011 to 2014 before a decade-long run at Dwight, where he ascended to an executive vice president role. At Arrow, Mandelbaum will focus heavily on negotiating multifamily loans while helping borrowers navigate alternative strategies. Among the multifamily deals he originated at Dwight was a $36 million bridge loan in 2023 for Latco Enterprises to refinance its Villa Annette Apartments property in Moreno Valley, Calif., CO first reported at the time. “I’m excited to join Arrow and work alongside a team with a strong track record across the commercial real estate capital markets,” Mandelbaum said in a statement. “My experience on the credit side has given me a firsthand understanding of how transactions are evaluated, structured and executed, and I look forward to applying that perspective to help Arrow’s clients navigate increasingly structured financing environments.” The addition of Mandelbaum comes on the heels of Arrow hiring Jeff Weinberg from Meridian Capital Group as a managing director, CO previously reported. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.

stories.title: Florida Tech Opens $96 Million Student Dorm
stories.excerpt: Florida Tech has opened the doors of a six-story, 556-bed student housing complex on the Melbourne campus. It was funded through $96.1 million in municipal bond financing. Dubbed Crimson Crossing, it was built using a Public-Private Partnership (P3) model with Servitas Development. It took 15 months to build. The majority of the apartment-style units in the complex will be four-bedroom, two-bathroom suites equipped with full kitchens. Amenities will include a classroom area, study and lounge spaces, a multipurpose room and two outdoor courtyards designed for dining and recreation. The need for more student housing is fueled by Florida Tech’s growing student body. Traditional and online student enrollment has increased more than 27% since 2019, reaching over 10,000 students in fall 2025. During that same timeframe, first-time-in-college students have jumped over 43%, and the fall-to-fall retention rate increased from 74.3% in 2022 to 83.3% in 2025. stories.title: The Fever’s Down, But New York’s Rent-Stabilized Market Is Still Ill
stories.excerpt: New York City’s rent-stabilized housing stock has an increasingly serious economic problem. For years, the operating expenses of these buildings have been rising much faster than their revenues. Insurance premiums, real estate taxes, water and sewer charges, fuel, labor, repairs and maintenance have all increased significantly, while the ability of owners to increase rents has been severely constrained. The Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019 eliminated or restricted many of the mechanisms owners previously used to recover investments in their buildings, and now we have a rent freeze layered on top of that. The result is not complicated. When expenses consistently grow faster than revenue, eventually the two lines cross. Robert Knakal. PHOTO: Patrick McMullan/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images New York City’s Article XI is increasingly being discussed as one possible solution. The program can provide an extraordinary property-tax benefit to qualifying buildings for as long as 40 years, replacing conventional real estate taxes with a substantially lower PILOT, or payment in lieu of taxes. For a distressed rent-stabilized building, the impact can be dramatic. A building paying 25 percent or more of its gross revenue in real estate taxes might see that burden reduced substantially. Suddenly, a property that was barely breaking even, or even losing money, can generate positive cash flow again. For an owner facing a mortgage maturity, foreclosure or the prospect of handing the keys back to the lender, Article XI can be a lifeline. But a lifeline is not a cure. Think about a patient suffering from a serious infection and running a dangerously high fever. You give the patient Tylenol. The fever comes down. The patient feels better. Everyone is relieved. stories.title: Every Industry Eventually Learns a Shared Language. Data Centers Are Next.
stories.excerpt: One question has stayed with me since my last column on data center disclosure: How do standards emerge in an industry where every project is different? It is an important question because nothing about today’s data center market looks standardized. Every project is different. Every community asks different questions. Every developer tells a slightly different story. Yet history suggests that industries almost never begin with standards. They grow into them. Suhail Y Tayeb. PHOTO: Courtesy NYU The reason is straightforward. As industries mature, inconsistent information becomes expensive. Investors, lenders, insurers, regulators and customers all reach the same conclusion. Comparing projects is easier when everyone speaks the same language. The pattern repeats itself across industries. Finance eventually adopted Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) because investors needed confidence that financial statements meant the same thing from one company to the next. The standards did not make companies identical. They made companies comparable. Real estate followed a similar path. Residential appraisers do not prepare a different report for every lender. Standardized appraisal forms such as the Uniform Residential Appraisal Report, also known as Form 1004, became common because investors buying mortgages needed comparable information. The form did not standardize houses. It standardized how houses were described. Green building tells the same story. LEED began as a voluntary certification developed by the U.S. Green Building Council. Developers pursued certification because tenants, investors and lenders increasingly viewed it as a credible signal of quality and performance. Only later did many municipalities incorporate LEED into procurement requirements, incentives and public policy.
